topic.title: One Phone Call Doubled the Load on This Walkway

title: The Hyatt Walkway Collapse: One Phone Call Doubled the Load
description:
In Kansas City, two steel walkways hung above a crowded hotel atrium on thin rods. Why did they fall?
This is the full cause chain from the federal investigation: a connection that was already too weak, a change agreed by phone during construction, a connection that nobody calculated, and the nut that pulled through its beam.
Then what the investigators measured in their lab, and the rule every engineer works under because of it.

CHAPTERS
0:00 The walkways and the question
0:44 The hotel
1:35 How it was meant to hold
2:41 The chain
4:47 The last minutes
5:31 The failure
6:36 What the investigators found
7:37 What changed

Sources: National Bureau of Standards, Investigation of the Kansas City Hyatt Regency Walkways Collapse; ASCE Civil Engineering magazine.
Based on official investigation reports and published sources. 3D scenes are reconstructions, not actual footage.

Report: US National Institute of Standards and Technology, nbsbuildingscience143, page 7 of 378, Public domain (US government work) (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/BSS/nbsbuildingscience143.pdf)
cta: Which link in the chain should have stopped it? Tell us in the comments

lines.text: Kansas City, 1981. Two steel walkways hang over a crowded hotel lobby, one directly above the other.
On the upper walkway, one nut and washer are holding far more than they were ever meant to.
At about 5 past 7 in the evening, the beam around that nut tears open.
In seconds, both walkways are on the floor.
Why? The investigators found the steel and the workmanship played no significant role. It was a chain of small decisions, and one of them was made over the phone.
This is how one small change on a drawing doubled the load, and why nobody caught it.
The Hyatt Regency walkway collapse.
The Hyatt Regency in Kansas City opened in 1980.
A 40-storey tower, a block of ballrooms, and between them a glass atrium about 15 m high.
Across that atrium ran three walkways, at the second, third and fourth floors.
The third was set off to one side. The fourth-floor walkway ran directly above the second.
No columns held them up over the lobby. Each one hung from the roof on thin steel rods.
Why hang them? Because a walkway floating in the air looks weightless, and it keeps the lobby floor clear for crowds.
For a year, they held. Nobody could see what was wrong with them.
So what was wrong from the very first day? To see it, you have to look inside one joint.
Under each walkway ran steel box beams. Each one was two 8-inch channels, welded toe to toe.
A rod came down from the roof, through a hole in the beam. Underneath, a nut and washer held the beam up.
Here is the weak spot. The rod passed through a hole drilled right where the two channels' edges met, along the weld.
So the whole weight pressed down through one washer onto two thin flange lips, held together by that weld. How much could that take?
What did the engineers draw? One long rod for both walkways.
It ran from the roof, through the fourth-floor beam, and straight on down through the second-floor beam.
Each beam sat on its own nut, so each nut carried only its own walkway.
Was that design safe? Not quite. The investigators found it reached only about 60% of the strength the Kansas City code expected.
So the drawing was already short. Then, during construction, someone asked a simple question.
The steel fabricator looked at that long rod and saw a problem.
How do you put a nut halfway up a rod that long? The rod would need thread most of its length, or the nut wound all the way up.
Two shorter rods were simpler. One from the roof to the fourth-floor beam. A second from that beam down to the second floor.
As reported, the fabricator asked for the change by telephone. The structural engineer agreed, on the understanding that a written request would follow.
As reported, the written request never came.
On paper the two joints look almost the same. They aren't.
With one rod, the lower walkway hangs from the roof. With two, it hangs from the upper walkway's beam.
Think of two climbers on one rope. Each holds the rope with their own hands. Now tie the lower climber to the upper one's harness instead.
Now the nut under the upper beam carries its own walkway, and the whole walkway below it.
The load on that connection essentially doubled.
So who calculated the new joint? Nobody did.
The fabricator was busy, and passed the drawings to an outside detailer.
As reported, the detailer believed the two-rod joint had already been designed, so he did no calculations on it.
Back at the engineers' office, a technician reviewed the drawings. The joint wasn't detailed on them, and nobody calculated it.
The engineer of record made spot checks, and put his seal on the drawings.
How could that happen? He was responsible for about 10 associate engineers, each running several projects at once.
Four links, each one small. And the walkways were already hanging by them when the hotel planned a party.
So far: a joint that was already weak, a change that doubled its load, and drawings that nobody calculated. What was still missing? A crowd.
Friday, July 17, 1981. A dance in the atrium.
By the evening, newspapers put the crowd at 1,500 to 2,000 people.
Some watched from the walkways above.
A television crew was filming. From its tape, investigators later counted about 63 people on the second and fourth-floor walkways.
Is that a heavy load? No. The building code expected walkways like these to carry far more people than that.
At 4 minutes past 7, the band came back from its break for a dance contest.
One minute later, under the upper walkway, one nut was about to let go.
It began at the east end of the fourth-floor walkway's middle box beam.
The rod held. The nut held. The beam around them did not.
The welded seam split, the flange bent open, and the nut and washer pulled straight through.
And with one hanger gone? The others took its share, and failed one after another.
The fourth-floor walkway fell onto the second, and both crashed to the lobby floor.
113 people died and 186 were injured. The federal report called it the most devastating structural collapse ever to take place in the United States.
The first call for help reached the fire department at 8 minutes past 7. By 19 past, rescuers were calling for cutting tools, and by 23 past, a forklift.
The third-floor walkway, hung on its own rods from the roof, stayed up.
Investigators had to answer one question. Was it the change alone, or was the joint always too weak?
The National Bureau of Standards took the case, and weighed pieces of the fallen walkways.
The decks were about 8% heavier than the drawings assumed. That was not enough to explain it.
So they built copies of the box beam joint and pulled on them until they broke.
They broke the way the real ones did. The weld split, and the nut punched through.
Then they did the sums. How much was that joint carrying on the night?
At most, about 31% of what a joint built to the code should have held.
And here is the turn. Under the original one-rod design, those same joints would have survived that night.
The original still fell short of the code. But it would have held.
With two rods, the report says, from the day they were built the walkways had only minimal capacity to resist their own weight.
For a year, people walked across a structure that could barely hold itself up.
In Missouri, the engineering board revoked the licences of 2 engineers involved, for gross negligence and misconduct.
The engineer of record argued that it was common practice to leave connections to the fabricator. Whose job was the joint?
In 1985, the American Society of Civil Engineers answered: the engineer of record is responsible for the design of every steel connection.
Since then, the engineer of record answers for every connection, and a change to one is meant to be checked before it is built.
Engineering students still study this joint. A rod, a nut, a washer, and one phone call.
So which link should have stopped it? The weak original joint, the phone call, the detailer, or the review and the seal?

promise: 'It wasn't bad steel, and it wasn't bad welding' (and the struck-out BAD WELDING card) overstates NBS BSS 143 s10.6: box beam weld penetration averaged below AWS D1.1-79; NBS concluded only that materials and workmanship played no significant role in initiating the collapse. Say that instead (e.g. 'The investigators found the steel and the workmanship played no significant role') and change the card to match.

who: 'So who checked the new joint? Nobody did.' contradicts NBS (shop drawings 'were reviewed by the contractor, structural engineer and architect', per their stamps) and the script's own review/seal beats. Sources say the connection was never calculated, not that nobody reviewed it: e.g. 'So who calculated the new joint? Nobody did.' The empty CHECKED box in who and promise-2 must become an unticked CONNECTION CALCS (or similar) line, since the drawings were stamped.

today: 'Today, a change to a connection goes back to the engineer who designed it, and it is checked before it is built' is stated as universal present practice, unsourced (connection design is still often delegated to the fabricator's engineer, with EOR review). Tie it to the source: e.g. 'Since then, the engineer of record answers for every connection, and a change to one is meant to be checked before it is built.'
